en: My courser, let Khan Bakay be your companion.
This journey there and back
I entrust to the one God.
Go in health and return unharmed.
Your poor mother here—
Do not make me lament, my son; return soon!”
Saying this, Kanykey,
Weeping, grieving, distraught,
To the unruly boy Manas left behind
Gave counsel, imploring him.
Unable to stand, weeping and crying out,
To the orphan she had gained at long last,
Your poor mother Kanykey
Gave her blessing, sobbing:
“Every saint and holy elder,
Protect my orphan!” she said.
Entrusting him, crying out,
She sent him toward Talas.
Telling many tales of what had happened,
While the leopard Manas lived,
Of what she herself had endured,
Recounting the deeds like an old tale,
While your mother Kanykey stood weeping,
The mother who had borne Manas,
An elder ninety-five years old,
Was herself a saint protected by Shai.
As a son she bore hero Manas,
Who became khan wherever his name was heard.
The enemies who fought him were destroyed.
Born and raised in Altay,
He was mighty among all the world's peoples.
The enemies who struggled with him were humbled.
As a daughter she bore a hero,
The daughter she bore, Kardygach,
Who stirred much trouble among the Chinese,
And suffered many humiliations.
Freed from the Chinese,
To Zharmanas of the humble people,
Down below, at the world's end, Zhelpinish,
She was given in marriage in Zhelpinish.
At that time Chiyrdy,
Her only orphan having grown,
Had her wish granted by God.
Surviving without perishing, Chiyrdy
Had reached ninety-five.
Her eyes were festering;
Her chest was wheezing.
Her twelve limbs and bones
Trembled without respite.
(My mountain-like Urmeke,
My mother who bore noble Khan Manas.
Called dead, yet not in a grave;
Called living, yet not counted among them.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Such is this shitty world.)
Wiping her eyes and crying out,
A golden staff in her hand,
She called her only Semetey:
“Turn your horse's head a moment;
I am your mother Chiyrdy.
Wait while I tell my sorrow!
When I die, I shall enter the white palace.
My orphan whom I gained at long last,
May I take your misfortunes upon myself;
I shall tell you much of my grief.
When your father Manas died,
Parted from her camel calf,
When your mother suffered humiliation,
God's sun in the sky was clouded over.
Upon the head of your poor mother here,
Sixty afflictions fell at once.
'How can I remain behind my morning star, Manas?
Let me follow my departing son.
This wretched life that God has not taken,
Let me offer it as a sacrifice;
Let me die thus,'
I said then, wretched soul.
My thoughts turned to dying,
To seeing the face of the next world!
When I looked at the lattice wall,
Of the bright dagger I had bought,
The handle came into view.
Your wretched mother here
Turned her heart toward death.
Seizing it by the handle,
Drawing it from its sheath,
To thrust the knife into my heart—
That was my thought, wretched soul.
With your father, the lion Manas,
At his feet, wretched soul,
To lie there like a stopper.
May I take your misfortunes upon myself;
You were then a nursing infant.
When poor Kanykey suffered grief,
When she was plunged into bitter hardship,
Tearing both her cheeks,
When your mother left you without nursing,
To cut myself open,
To your father, hero Manas,
To remain together with him,
When I went to his feet,
My orphan in swaddling clothes,
You pulled out your hands and flailed,
Tugging at my knife,
Feeling for my breast.
Orphan, you laughed, spreading your fingers.
I wished to die of my grief.
I did not die, my foal,
Because you, Semetey, were there.
Looking into your eyes,
My foal, I made you my support.
I could not give up my life,
My foal, because you were there.
I did not spill my blood.
My hoof left by the winged steed,
My unruly, barren noble horse,
My pennon fixed upon the spear,
My gift left by generous Manas,
My plump darling, my gray-and-white goshawk,
My gray goshawk, my morning star,
Praying that my only one should stay safe,
I lamented to the one God.
My orphan, whom have I besides you?
Go on your journey to Talas,
And recite the Quran
For your father, Sultan Manas.
May your journey be safe.
People of Bukhara, hear my words!
My orphan is leaving for Talas.
O God, I entrust him to you alone!
My orphan whom I gained at long last,
Take ten days to go there;
Stay among the people another ten days;
Take another ten days to return.
The allotted time is thirty days;
You shall return in thirty days.
If you do not come within thirty days,
Of your wretched mother here
You will see the day of death!
All the common people of Bukhara,
Say 'Amen!' and spread your hands.
Today I have closed my mouth in fasting.
For thirty days I shall pray,
Let me perform whatever good deed I can.
Before thirty days are past,
If my orphan returns,
I shall see the people's faces.
If he is later than thirty days,
People, I shall see the face of the next world!
Amen! God, the hero is alone.
Among horses, the white-headed winged steed;
Almambet and Chubak, their names paired,
God, set his undertaking right;
My orphan goes forth—protect him!
Your orphan is coming; watch over him.
Ajybay and Bakay, the two khans,
Two souls born lions,
My orphan is coming; watch over him!
Forty chiltens, Kyzyr and Ilyas,
My only one goes forth, entrusted to you.
Amen!” she said, spreading her hands.
Both his mothers spread their hands alike.
Their hearts distracted,
Tears pouring from their eyes:
“That dear bird called the wild duck,
Do not let the goshawk devour it.
That unruly boy we rely upon—
Do not let his people say he is dead!
O God, do not let a bird devour the swan.
The orphan granted us by fortune—
Do not let word come from Talas that he is dead!”
Voicing their sorrow, striding forward,
For the orphan left by the generous hero,
Both his mothers wept,
Entrusting him to the Creator.
While his mother Chiyrdy stood weeping,
The city of Bukhara wept tears of blood,
All the people wept,
The holy man in a white turban wept,
The mullah who read his lessons wept.
His grandfather, Khan Temir,
The mighty khan of Bukhara, wept.
When Semetey set out for Talas,
All those people wept:
“The hero's only son was a lion;
From famous Sultan Manas
He was the hero left behind.
He has no brother following him;
He himself was born an only child.
May this orphan not perish;
May he go in safety!”
Then the city of Bukhara cried out;
All the people,
Raising their hands and sobbing,
Gave their blessing, crying out.
“If my appointed death comes, I shall die;
For my departed father Manas,
I shall go and recite the Quran,” he said.
The mount beneath him
Was Khan Temir's winged steed;
What he held in his hand
Was Ismayyl's steel blade.
The banner fluttered in his hand.
Your orphan left by Manas,
With Aktulpar beneath him,
The hero rode toward Talas, shining.
Swiftly invoking Baabedin,
For his father, generous Manas,
Pledging a white-hoofed mare in prayer,
He left Bukhara and took the road.
Without turning back, he rode steadily,
Crossing ridges veiled in pale haze,
Traversing beautifully formed country.
The boy traveled without wavering,
Going far, not sparing his horse.
To the great Ak-Chiy of spacious Bukhara,
For one riding a mighty winged steed,
For a mortal traveling without idling,
It was a six-day journey.
They called it Munara Ak-Chiy.
He traversed that Ak-Chiy;
The jutting mountain's shoulder
Your orphan crossed over.
“These were mother Kanykey's words:
'If you visit it, a great shrine,
Your mother's from her girlhood,
It is Keng-Kolchuk,' she said.
When her treasure was scattered,
My mother, exhausted and weeping,
Carrying me, the orphan,
When she fled Talas on foot,
With two skins of milk
And two fat working horses,
All their provisions ran out,
And only one bone of meat remained.
My grandmother Chiyrdy wept in anguish;
The widows, with that one bone of meat,
Called on God and pleaded.
These were my mother Kanykey's words:
My wretched mother, at Keng-Kolchuk,
'I cast a divination,' she said.
'If you look, this is your omen:
Your mother's Keng-Kolchuk,
Bubbling and brimming with water,
Overflows,' she said.
'From its breath, Keng-Kolchuk
Surges over,' she said.
'A grove of plane trees
Surrounds it,' she said.
These were mother Kanykey's words.
Everything she spoke of is here.
Ah, my mother Kanykey
Is a soul endowed with sacred power.
A black stone stands beside the water;
On the black stone is writing.
When I read the writing,
